'TypeScript Plan Review

planning/frontend/FRONTEND_INTEGRATION_IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md (lines 997-1080) claims only 1,112 errors remain and phases 4‑6 are “production-ready”, yet docs/TYPE_SAFETY_MEASUREMENT_BASELINE.md (lines 1-74) establishes a newer 2,319‑error baseline measured with tsconfig.json. The plan never reconciles the two counts or explains which config CI uses, so merge decisions are being made on stale numbers.
frontend/tsconfig.prod.json (lines 62-93) only compiles a hand-picked list of files and omits whole directories that were moved during the merge (e.g., StoryBuilder now lives at frontend/src/components/story-builder/StoryBuilder.tsx (line 1) and every store lives under frontend/src/store, neither of which match any include glob). Builds therefore “pass” while large sections of the app—and their TypeScript errors—are never type-checked, which explains why the CFN loop thought it was fixing everything. Before merging anything else we need a prod config that extends the base config and covers src/**/*.
The merge plan keeps the entire AI/chat/photo-editing surface in src/components/ai and wires those files into tsconfig.prod (frontend/tsconfig.prod.json (lines 72-75)) even though the shipping UI (frontend/src/pages/EpicProgressDemo.tsx (lines 25-112)) never renders them. That means dead, experimental code is blocking compilation instead of living behind a feature flag or in a demo/ package. We’re effectively merging demo frontends into main without any gating.
Both the plan and the handoff instruct engineers to run npx tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.prod.json 2>&1 | grep "error TS" | wc -l (planning/frontend/FRONTEND_INTEGRATION_IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md (lines 1032-1041), TYPESCRIPT_COMPILATION_HANDOFF.md (lines 309-354)). On Windows (and in most CI runners) grep/wc aren’t available, and the command assumes you’re already cd’d into frontend. This is the “measurement methodology failure” in action—different people literally ran different commands.
Duplicate-export cleanup was only partially done: frontend/src/types/chat.ts (lines 331-351) still re-exports interfaces that are already declared with export interface, keeping the TS2484 errors alive. The plan celebrates fixing photoTypes.ts, but the same pattern migrated into chat.ts and types/enhanced-blocks.ts, so the loop just chased the problem around.
Recommended Fix Strategy

Replace the bespoke include list with a layered config: have frontend/tsconfig.prod.json extend ./tsconfig.json, keep include: ["src/**/*"], and only exclude the folders we explicitly don’t ship (tests, deprecated, demo packages). Then add a focused tsconfig.experimental.json that does include src/components/ai/**/* so that team can iterate without blocking prod. This instantly surfaces the real error set and lets merges fail when critical folders regress.
Introduce a simple cross-platform measurement script (e.g., scripts/count-ts-errors.mjs) that runs npx tsc --noEmit --project frontend/tsconfig.prod.json and counts errors via Node, writing the count plus a timestamp to docs/measurements/*.md. Wire that script into CI so merge checks use a single source of truth.
Gate unfinished feature sets: move src/components/ai, Gemini services, and related stores into frontend/experiments/ or wrap their exports in a process.env.VITE_ENABLE_AI check so they aren’t compiled (or even imported) in prod bundles until TypeScript is green. Doing this for the chat/photo editors immediately drops several hundred errors without deleting code.
Attack the remaining errors by category instead of by file: run npx tsc --noEmit --pretty false | rg -o "error TS\\d{4}" | sort | uniq -c to rank error families, then assign owners. Start with the global issues called out in the handoff (duplicate exports, import type misuse, lucide icon typings) because each fix clears dozens of files at once.
Once tsconfig.prod and the gating strategy are fixed, flip noImplicitAny to true in frontend/tsconfig.json and let Vite keep using the stricter config locally (npm run typecheck already points at prod config). That keeps the merge process honest going forward.
Suggested next steps: 1) update tsconfig.prod.json to extend the base config and run the new error-count script to establish a trustworthy baseline; 2) move or flag the AI components so production builds only compile the code we actually ship; 3) schedule a focused duplicate-export/BlockType cleanup pass before re-running any automated fixing loop.

I asked our team for feedback, you can ignore timeline comments. Here it is: Findings

No Windows setup story. The Quick Start only tells engineers to read architecture/risk docs (planning/windows/README.md:65-69) even though the target state depends on heavy native modules such as ioredis and better-sqlite3 (planning/windows/README.md:27-28). There are zero deliverables for installing Redis/SQLite services on Windows, provisioning node-gyp/Visual Studio Build Tools, handling antivirus exclusions, or packaging these prerequisites for users, so “native Windows support” would still fail on a clean machine.

Script migration plan ignores CLI dependencies. The plan tracks raw counts (289 bash scripts, 409 redis-cli invocations, etc.) and simply states that 70 % become TypeScript while 30 % get PowerShell twins (planning/windows/README.md:17-33, 74-83), plus a “top 20” migration in sprint 4.1 (planning/windows/epic-cross-platform-support.json:368-381). There is no inventory of GNU tools used inside those scripts (sed, awk, jq, rsync, SSH, etc.) or any strategy for replacing them on Windows, so even rewritten entry points may still depend on missing Unix binaries.

WSL fallback assumes infrastructure that may not exist. Decision 4 promises an automatic fallback to WSL so Windows users “just work” (planning/windows/README.md:93-96), yet the epic only detects whether WSL is present (planning/windows/epic-cross-platform-support.json:45) and never provisions it, checks version compatibility, or guides users through enabling the Windows feature. Without detection + install flows or user messaging, the promised safety net is unreliable.

Job Object story is internally inconsistent. The goal and business case hinge on “memory leak prevention via Windows Job Objects” (planning/windows/README.md:10, planning/windows/epic-cross-platform-support.json:19), sprint 3.1 even requires a WindowsProcessManager with Job Object support (planning/windows/epic-cross-platform-support.json:248-257), yet backlog item 001 explicitly defers implementing native Job Object bindings because the current plan only has a taskkill fallback (planning/windows/epic-cross-platform-support.json:587-591). Either the acceptance criteria need to drop Job Objects or the backlog item must move into the main scope.

Schedule assumes heroic throughput. Examples: a 400‑line Redis coordinator + tests in 2 days (planning/windows/epic-cross-platform-support.json:129-143), a 600‑line cross-platform process manager with resource limits in another 2 days (planning/windows/epic-cross-platform-support.json:248-257), and a 500‑line shell executor plus migration of the top 20 scripts in 2 days (planning/windows/epic-cross-platform-support.json:368-381). Each of those alone typically takes more than a week when you factor in design, reviews, manual testing across four OSes, and rollout. The four-week epic therefore understates effort and risk.

Suggested next steps

Add explicit tasks for Windows prerequisite installation (Redis, SQLite, node-gyp toolchain, optional WSL install) and user-facing documentation/scripts.
Inventory the commands used inside the 289 scripts, decide which ones must be reimplemented, and schedule that work before declaring Windows readiness.
Reconcile the Job Object plan vs backlog and re-estimate sprints with realistic buffers (or split the epic).

Agent image sets only three baked env vars and relies on scripts/docker-agent-init.sh to re-read REDIS_HOST/REDIS_PORT/TASK_ID/AGENT_TYPE, so every consumer must remember to pre-set those names separately from the Dockerfile defaults Dockerfile.agent (lines 47-58), scripts/docker-agent-init.sh (lines 6-68).
Coordinator image bakes its own defaults for Redis, network, memory, and agent image, then coordinator.js re-reads them and selectively forwards pieces of process.env into spawned containers Dockerfile.coordinator (lines 38-52), docker/coordinator/src/coordinator.js (lines 23-37) & 286-302.
Orchestrator image expects /app/container-mode-detection.sh and only understands CFN_REDIS_URL, which diverges from the REDIS_HOST/PORT contract used by the agent stack; the referenced script is never copied into the image (it only exists in Dockerfile.agent.stabilized) Dockerfile.orchestrator (lines 30-65), Dockerfile.agent.stabilized (lines 26-76).
Problems

Redis configuration spans three different names (REDIS_HOST/PORT, CFN_REDIS_URL, REDIS_URL), so changing a host or port requires editing every Dockerfile and shell script; the agent init script ignores CFN_REDIS_URL while the orchestrator ignores REDIS_HOST/PORT scripts/docker-agent-init.sh (lines 6-33), Dockerfile.orchestrator (lines 38-41).
Coordinator never sets the TASK_ID and AGENT_TYPE variables the agent boot script expects, so it falls back to unknown and writes opaque Redis keys scripts/docker-agent-init.sh (lines 6-15), docker/coordinator/src/coordinator.js (lines 286-301).
Every image inlines its own defaults, so there is no single place to update values like AGENT_IMAGE, NETWORK_NAME, or memory budgets Dockerfile.agent (lines 47-58), Dockerfile.coordinator (lines 38-45), Dockerfile.orchestrator (lines 56-59).
The orchestrator entrypoint sources a file that is never copied into the image, so it cannot share whatever mode-detection logic the agent build is using Dockerfile.orchestrator (lines 30-41).
Standardization Proposal

Define one canonical “runtime contract” file (docker/runtime/cfn-runtime.contract.yml) that lists every variable once with name, default, scope (agent/coordinator/orchestrator/shared), and any legacy aliases. Example sections: Redis (CFN_REDIS_HOST, CFN_REDIS_PORT, CFN_REDIS_URL), coordinator tuning (CFN_COORDINATOR_MEMORY_BUDGET, CFN_COORDINATOR_MAX_ITERATIONS), agent metadata (CFN_AGENT_IMAGE, CFN_AGENT_ITERATION_CAP), orchestrator flags (CFN_MODE, CFN_DOCKER_CONTAINER).
Add a generator script (scripts/generate-cfn-runtime-env.ts) that reads the contract and emits three artifacts:
docker/runtime/cfn-runtime.env for Compose/docker run --env-file.
docker/runtime/cfn-runtime.sh, a sourceable script that exports every canonical variable plus backwards-compatible aliases (e.g., set CFN_REDIS_HOST once, derive REDIS_HOST, build CFN_REDIS_URL if missing).
docker/runtime/cfn-runtime.json, so Node code (coordinator spawn logic) can import the same list instead of filtering process.env.
Update Dockerfiles to copy and source the same artifacts:
Add ARG CFN_RUNTIME_ENV=docker/runtime/cfn-runtime.sh and COPY $CFN_RUNTIME_ENV /opt/cfn/runtime-env.sh && chmod +x /opt/cfn/runtime-env.sh.
Prepend each entrypoint (scripts/docker-agent-init.sh, coordinator bootstrap, orchestrator entrypoint) with source /opt/cfn/runtime-env.sh, so defaults and aliases stay in sync automatically.
Copy scripts/mode-detection.sh once to /opt/cfn/container-mode-detection.sh and have both agent and orchestrator source it, removing the bespoke inline script from Dockerfile.agent.stabilized.
Refactor coordinator runtime logic to honor the canonical names and to forward them consistently:
Change the CONFIG object to prefer CFN_* keys while still honoring legacy aliases, and read the generated JSON so it knows exactly which keys to inject into agent containers docker/coordinator/src/coordinator.js (lines 23-37).
When spawning agents, add TASK_ID/AGENT_TYPE from the same config and use the JSON list instead of ad hoc prefix filters, so the agent init script stops defaulting to “unknown” docker/coordinator/src/coordinator.js (lines 286-302), scripts/docker-agent-init.sh (lines 6-15).
Document the workflow in docker/README-BUILD-PROCESS.md, add npm run docker:env-sync (invokes the generator), and teach compose/test scripts to load docker/runtime/cfn-runtime.env rather than duplicating exports.
Rollout Steps

Commit the contract + generator, add "docker:env-sync": "tsx scripts/generate-cfn-runtime-env.ts" to package.json, and run it once to produce the env artifacts.
Amend Dockerfile.agent, Dockerfile.coordinator, and Dockerfile.orchestrator to copy /opt/cfn/runtime-env.sh and /opt/cfn/container-mode-detection.sh, and update the entrypoint scripts to source them before doing any work.
Update docker/coordinator/src/coordinator.js to consume the canonical env map/JSON and to pass the standardized variables to every agent container.
Regenerate the env artifacts, rebuild all three images, and smoke-test Redis connectivity plus agent spawn flow (ensuring the init script now sees the correct TASK_ID, AGENT_TYPE, and Redis host/port).
Refresh docs/tests (docker/README-BUILD-PROCESS.md, tests/docker/production-agent-orchestrator.js, etc.) to point to the new single source of truth.
Once this is in place, updating something like the Redis endpoint or the agent image tag becomes a one-line change in cfn-runtime.contract.yml followed by npm run docker:env-sync, and every Docker build, compose file, and script will pick it up automatically.

Investigation Team

Tiered sync scheduling (hourly Tier 1, weekly Tier 2, monthly Tier 3) with API call budgeting is clearly laid out, and the projected ~5k–9k monthly calls stay well under the 359k limit documented in the plan (migration-plan/TMO_API_MIGRATION_PLAN.md (line 47), migration-plan/TMO_API_MIGRATION_PLAN.md (line 110)).
Comprehensive staging + metadata design (per-entity staging tables, sync_metadata, sync_execution_log, helper functions) provides the controls needed for incremental merges and auditability (migration-plan/staging-tables-schema.sql (line 12), migration-plan/staging-tables-schema.sql (line 41)).
The plan prescribes cron-friendly runbooks for each tier and an explicit derived-table rebuild phase after Tier 1, so dashboards can stay aligned with freshly ingested facts (migration-plan/TMO_API_MIGRATION_PLAN.md (line 241), migration-plan/TMO_API_MIGRATION_PLAN.md (line 282)).
Current ingestion tooling maps exported brokerview_*.txt views directly into Supabase tables, meaning the migration must continue to satisfy those view-level contracts—not just the base TMO entities (supabase-full-file-processing/nsc_processor.py (line 45)).
The Supabase target schema already expects enriched loan columns like OtherPayment, Reserve, Impound, and DaysLate, so the API solution has to either supply or recompute the same derived values (supabase-schema.db (line 306)).
Verification Team

The on-prem brokerview_loans view that feeds Supabase joins TDS Loans with wraps, split amounts, and impound/reserve aggregations; none of those source tables or equivalent API endpoints appear in the migration plan, so fetching only GetLoansByTimestamp will omit fields currently persisted in loans (on-prem-queries/brokerview_loans.sql (line 14), on-prem-queries/brokerview_total_wraps.sql (line 13), on-prem-queries/brokerview_sum_impound.sql (line 13)). Without an alternative, dashboards depending on OtherPayment, TrustAmount, Reserve, or Impound will regress.
Conversations are downstream views that join call notes to borrower identity (on-prem-queries/brokerview_conversations_borrower.sql (line 13)), yet the only documented API is the per-loan GetLoanConversations/{Account} with no timestamp filters (TMO API.postman_collection.json (line 7639)). The plan merely says “manual tracking” for Tier 1 conversations (migration-plan/TMO_API_MIGRATION_PLAN.md (line 56)) but never defines hash-based deduping or per-account checkpoints, so it cannot guarantee non-duplicated metrics in conversations (supabase-schema.db (line 99)).
Attachments (Tier 3) and borrower refreshes (Tier 2) both depend on record-by-record endpoints (GetLoanAttachments, GetLenderAttachments) which require one HTTP call per account (TMO API.postman_collection.json (line 1269)). The plan budgets just 10–50 calls/month for attachments (migration-plan/TMO_API_MIGRATION_PLAN.md (line 78)), but with hundreds of active loans the actual call count could explode unless further filtered logic is defined.

he hanging isn’t coming from jest.useFakeTimers() at all—the leak is in the cleanup helpers that run after you switch back to real timers, so Jest never gets a chance to drain them.
tests/metrics-logger.test.ts (line 91) – cleanupTestDatabase races dbService.disconnect() against setTimeout(..., 2000) but never clears the timeout when the disconnect wins. Every afterEach therefore leaves a real 2‑second timeout handle alive, and the last one keeps Jest waiting until it finally fires.
tests/utils/cleanup.ts (line 158), tests/utils/cleanup.ts (line 186), tests/utils/cleanup.ts (line 224) – all three of the “force close” races inside TestCleanupManager do the same thing with 5‑second timers. Because jest.useRealTimers() is called before cleanup.cleanupAll(), those timers are created with the native timer APIs, escape Jest’s control, and keep the Node event loop open indefinitely if the losing promises never resolve (or at least for 5 seconds if they do).
The cleanup manager’s own clearTimers() only clears timers that were explicitly tracked via trackTimer(), so these internal fallback timers are invisible to it. That’s why the suite still hangs even though you call jest.runOnlyPendingTimers()/jest.clearAllTimers() in afterEach.
To fix it, store the timeout handle and clear it once either branch resolves, or wrap the pattern in a helper:
async function withTimeout<T>(promise: Promise<T>, ms: number) {   let timeout: NodeJS.Timeout;   try {     const timeoutPromise = new Promise<never>((_, reject) => {       timeout = setTimeout(() => reject(new Error(`Timed out after ${ms} ms`)), ms);     });     return await Promise.race([promise, timeoutPromise]);   } finally {     if (timeout) clearTimeout(timeout);   } }
Use that helper (or at least clearTimeout(timeoutId) in a finally) in cleanupTestDatabase and in each Promise.race inside TestCleanupManager. Once those fallback timers are cleaned up, the suite will exit immediately without the “keeps running forever” behavior. Consider rerunning with npx jest tests/metrics-logger.test.ts --runInBand --detectOpenHandles to verify the open handles disappear after applying t
